citations.quote:
Define the linear map $\kappa:V\to M_2(\mathbb C)$ by

$$\kappa(p)=p^0I_2+p^1\sigma_1+p^2\sigma_2+p^3\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}p^0+p^3&p^1-ip^2\\p^1+ip^2&p^0-p^3\end{pmatrix},$$

For a matrix $M$ whose image is one-dimensional (rank one), a spinor factorization is a pair $(\lambda,\widetilde\lambda)\in(\mathbb C^2\setminus\{0\})\times(\widetilde{\mathbb C}^2\setminus\{0\})$ satisfying $M_{a\dot a}=\lambda_a\widetilde\lambda_{\dot a}$.

derivations.claim: Direct expansion gives $\det\kappa(p)=(p^0)^2-(p^1)^2-(p^2)^2-(p^3)^2=h(p,p)=0$. The explicit inverse formula in [F4] shows $\kappa(p)\ne0$ because $p\ne0$. A nonzero $2\times2$ matrix with determinant zero has rank one.

Choose a nonzero column $v$ of $\kappa(p)$. Rank one means each of its two columns is a scalar multiple $a_{\dot a}v$; setting $\lambda=v$ and $\widetilde\lambda_{\dot a}=a_{\dot a}$ gives the factorization required by [F3]. Both factors are nonzero because their product matrix is nonzero.

Any second factorization has the same one-dimensional column space, so $\lambda'=t\lambda$ for a unique nonzero scalar $t$. Equality of the outer products then gives $\widetilde\lambda'=t^{-1}\widetilde\lambda$ by comparing a nonzero component of $\lambda$. This proves uniqueness of the class.

boundaries.reason: The statement concerns one specified nonzero momentum, not an empty momentum family.
The zero vector is expressly excluded because its matrix has rank zero.

boundaries.evidence: step 2.1 covers the case where only one matrix column is nonzero; choose that column.
Steps 1.1 and 2.1 use only nonzero rank one, including matrices with a zero column.

boundaries.reason: No interval, limit, or endpoint is used.

boundaries.evidence: step 2.1 chooses one nonzero column from a finite two-column matrix; no arbitrary-family choice is used.

boundaries.reason: The statement is an existence and uniqueness assertion, not a biconditional.
The statement is an existence and uniqueness assertion, not a biconditional.

risk_review.notes: Finite check: for p=(1,1,0,0), h(p,p)=0 and kappa(p)=[[1,1],[1,1]]=(1,1)^T(1,1). The proof covers every nonzero null p and proves uniqueness up to the stated rescaling.

citations.quote: For a matrix $M$ whose image is one-dimensional (rank one), a spinor factorization is a pair $(\lambda,\widetilde\lambda)\in(\mathbb C^2\setminus\{0\})\times(\widetilde{\mathbb C}^2\setminus\{0\})$ satisfying $M_{a\dot a}=\lambda_a\widetilde\lambda_{\dot a}$.
Thus for every nonzero $p$ with $h(p,p)=0$, $\kappa(p)$ has a spinor factorization.

derivations.claim: The finite collection of initial spinor factors exists by [F4]; since $n$ is finite, choose them successively without an arbitrary-family choice principle. In matrix coordinates, $\kappa(p_i(z))=(\lambda_i+z\lambda_j)\widetilde\lambda_i=\kappa(p_i)+z\lambda_j\widetilde\lambda_i$ and $\kappa(p_j(z))=\lambda_j(\widetilde\lambda_j-z\widetilde\lambda_i)=\kappa(p_j)-z\lambda_j\widetilde\lambda_i$. Each shifted matrix is an outer product by [F1], hence has determinant zero; [F3] and [F2] then give nullness, and the two added terms cancel. Thus $\sum_a p_a(z)=0$.

Set $r_\alpha=\operatorname{Res}_{z=z_\alpha}A(z)$. The rational function $A(z)-\sum_{\alpha=1}^m r_\alpha/(z-z_\alpha)$ has no finite pole, so it is a polynomial; it tends to zero at infinity by [A2], so that polynomial is zero. Evaluating the resulting partial-fraction identity at $z=0$ gives $A(0)=-\sum_\alpha r_\alpha/z_\alpha$.

Since $z_\alpha\ne0$, the factor $1/z$ is regular there and $\operatorname{Res}_{z=z_\alpha}(A(z)/z)=r_\alpha/z_\alpha$. This proves the residue form. Under [A3], substitute each stated factorization for $r_\alpha$ to obtain the claimed recursion. No contour or large-z model estimate is used beyond the explicit decay hypothesis.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.2 gives A(0)=0 when there are no finite poles and A tends to zero at infinity.
The Statement requires regularity at z=0 and every listed pole z_alpha≠0; evaluation at zero in step 1.2 is therefore valid.
For A(z)=1/(z-1), the single residue gives -1 and A(0)=-1, matching step 1.2.
The Statement excludes coincident or higher-order poles by requiring distinct simple poles.
The hypotheses separately control z=0 and the limit at infinity; step 1.2 uses both.
The proof in step 1.2 uses the finite pole list and no choice principle.

boundaries.reason: The theorem gives a direct identity, not an equivalence.
The theorem gives a direct identity, not an equivalence.

risk_review.notes: Finite checks: A(z)=1/(z-1) yields A(0)=-1=-Res_1(A/z); a constant nonzero A violates the decay hypothesis and is handled by the B-page counterexample. Model rationality, factorization and decay are not proved here.

citations.quote: For a matrix $M$ whose image is one-dimensional (rank one), a spinor factorization is a pair $(\lambda,\widetilde\lambda)\in(\mathbb C^2\setminus\{0\})\times(\widetilde{\mathbb C}^2\setminus\{0\})$ satisfying $M_{a\dot a}=\lambda_a\widetilde\lambda_{\dot a}$.
Define angle and square brackets by $\langle\lambda r\rangle=\epsilon^{ab}\lambda_a r_b$ and $[\widetilde\lambda\widetilde r]=\epsilon^{\dot a\dot b}\widetilde\lambda_{\dot a}\widetilde r_{\dot b}$.
Thus for every nonzero $p$ with $h(p,p)=0$, $\kappa(p)$ has a spinor factorization.

derivations.claim: The factorization exists by [F4]. For undotted references, put $w^a=r^a/\langle\lambda r\rangle-s^a/\langle\lambda s\rangle$. Then $\lambda_aw^a=1-1=0$ by [F3]. The nonzero covector $\lambda_a$ has a one-dimensional kernel. Since the alternating tensor is invertible, $\lambda^a$ is nonzero and lies in that kernel; hence $w^a=c\lambda^a$ for some $c\in\mathbb C$. Substitution in the displayed polarization formula gives $E_+(p;r)-E_+(p;s)=\sqrt2c\lambda^a\widetilde\lambda^{\dot a}$, which is a scalar multiple of the momentum tensor.

For dotted references, put $\widetilde w^{\dot a}=\widetilde r^{\dot a}/[\widetilde\lambda\widetilde r]-\widetilde s^{\dot a}/[\widetilde\lambda\widetilde s]$. Then $\widetilde\lambda_{\dot a}\widetilde w^{\dot a}=1-1=0$ by [F3]. The kernel is spanned by $\widetilde\lambda^{\dot a}$ because the dotted alternating tensor is invertible, so $\widetilde w^{\dot a}=d\widetilde\lambda^{\dot a}$ and $E_-(p;\widetilde r)-E_-(p;\widetilde s)=\sqrt2d\lambda^a\widetilde\lambda^{\dot a}$, again proportional to $p$.

The explicit inverse formula in [F5] makes $\kappa$ a linear isomorphism, and each alternating tensor has determinant one, so the raised-index Pauli map is also an isomorphism. Each tensor identity therefore gives the same proportionality for the associated four-vectors. Pairing either difference with $J$ gives a scalar multiple of $h(p,J)=0$ under [F2, A2]. Thus both polarization contractions are reference independent.

boundaries.reason: Two admissible references are compared; an empty reference set is not in the statement.
The zero momentum is excluded because it has no nonzero spinor-helicity representative.

boundaries.evidence: When the two references agree, the normalized difference in steps 1.1 and 1.2 is zero.
The Statement and A1 exclude a reference proportional to the momentum spinor because its denominator would vanish; step 1.1 handles all remaining references.

boundaries.reason: No interval or limiting endpoint is involved.

boundaries.evidence: steps 1.1 and 2.1 use only the explicitly given finite spinor vectors and no choice principle.

boundaries.reason: The proposition gives a conditional implication, not a biconditional.
The proposition gives a conditional implication, not a biconditional.

risk_review.notes: Finite check: for lambda=(1,0), references r=(0,1) and s=(1,1) have nonzero angle denominators; the normalized difference is proportional to lambda. The same kernel proof treats all admissible references. Current conservation remains an explicit input.

citations.quote: Assume $A$ is regular at $z=0$, has distinct simple finite poles $z_1,\ldots,z_m\ne0$ and no other finite poles, and $A(z)\to0$ as $z\to\infty$.

derivations.claim: The constant $A(z)=c$ is rational, regular at $0$, and has no finite poles. Hence every finite-pole residue vanishes and the proposed boundary-free sum equals $0$.
But $A(0)=c\ne0$. At infinity $A(z)/z=c/z$, so by [A2] the residue at infinity is $-c$ and the boundary correction is $c$. Omitting it gives the contradiction.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 is exactly the empty finite-pole set; its residue sum is zero.
A1 requires c≠0; if c=0, the example would not contradict the proposed rule.
The example is one nonzero constant coefficient, evaluated directly in steps 1.1 and 2.1.
The coefficient has no finite poles or degeneracies; its only omitted contribution is at infinity in step 2.1.
step 2.1 computes the nonzero boundary correction at infinity while A(0)=c.

boundaries.reason: No choices or indexed families occur in this explicit constant example.
The counterexample refutes an implication, not a biconditional.
The counterexample refutes an implication, not a biconditional.

risk_review.notes: Finite exact check: with c=1, A(0)=1 and the finite residue sum is 0; A(z)/z=1/z has boundary correction 1. This is a formal scalar contact coefficient, not a claim about a full interacting theory.
